title: Exertion (Kern ch. 12)
hook: the bodhisattvas vow to teach the sutra in hard times; Mahapajapati and Yasodhara are given promises

segments.voice: Yesterday, a young girl from under the sea offered a jewel and awakened while two senior figures doubted her. Your line: in an instant. Whose answer surprised you? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-seven.

Here's a promise that comes with a warning label. A crowd of bodhisattvas stands before the Buddha and says: after you're gone, we'll keep teaching this sutra. Then, in the same breath, they describe exactly how bad it will be. People will be proud and hard to reach. They'll insult us. They'll threaten us. Some will throw us out. We'll keep going anyway. It's the kind of vow a person makes with eyes open, after reading the forecast. And tucked into the same chapter, two women who have been watching all of this get a promise of their own. Today: exertion.
screen: `A PROMISE WITH A WARNING LABEL.` → `IT WILL BE BAD.` → `WE'LL KEEP GOING.`

segments.voice: First, the vow. Two bodhisattvas, Bhaishajyaraja, the Medicine King, and Mahapratibhana, with their companions, promise to keep and teach this sutra after the Buddha's death, in an age when people will be hard to train. Then monks who've already received promises speak up too, and vow to teach it in other worlds. Second, Mahaprajapati, called Mahapajapati in Pali. She is the Buddha's aunt, and she stands with a great company of nuns, gazing at him. The Buddha notices the look. He asks her, in paraphrase: why look at me so sadly? Are you thinking I haven't named you? Then he names her. She too will become a Buddha, he says, and the nuns with her. Third, Yasodhara, the mother of Rahula. She thinks to herself: he still hasn't mentioned my name. And he does. Her own future buddhahood, spoken in front of everyone. Both women are glad, and both vow to teach the sutra too. Fourth, the hard part. The Buddha looks at the bodhisattvas in silence, and they understand what he's asking. So they answer in verse. In the fearful time to come, they say, people will abuse us, threaten us with sticks and swords, and call us heretics. Some of the proud ones wearing robes will mock us and drive us out. We'll bear it. We don't cling to body or life; we care for the path. That's exertion in this chapter: not a burst of energy on a good morning. It's the decision to keep going when the conditions are named and they're bad. And in the middle of all that, the women who had been watching from the side are seen, and named.
screen: `WE'LL TEACH IT WHEN IT'S HARD.` · `MAHAPRAJAPATI, LOOKING UP.` · `YASODHARA, NOT YET NAMED.` · `INSULTS, STICKS, AND NO TURNING BACK.` · then, large: `IN HARD TIMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: keep going in a hard time. Settle, and feel your feet or your seat. Let the breath come in and go out. Bring to mind one hard thing in your life right now. Don't solve it. Just name it, plainly, the way the bodhisattvas named the bad times ahead. Then find one small piece of it you can keep doing: one call, one page, one walk, one meal cooked. Hold that small piece, breath by breath. That's enough for today. The bell holds the time.
Exertion. In chapter twelve, the vow to keep teaching when the times are named and they're hard, and two women seen and given their promise. Today's word.
Your line: in hard times. Today, do the next small piece of something hard, without waiting for it to get easier. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: In Mahayana communities that keep the Lotus Sutra, the bodhisattvas' vow in this chapter is recited as a model of patient effort, and Mahaprajapati and Yasodhara are remembered as receiving their own promise of buddhahood.

original.note: Sanskrit: energy, effort, steady exertion; one of the perfections a bodhisattva practices.

trapdoor: what you thought: exertion means a burst of energy.
what it means: a vow to keep teaching after the Buddha is gone, with the hard times named in advance.
what a scholar hears: the same chapter that pictures a fearful age to come also gives Mahaprajapati and Yasodhara their own promise of buddhahood.

notes: Chapter paraphrased from Kern (1884) ch. 12, not quoted (wording unverified). Check: Bhaishajyaraja and Mahapratibhana vow; predicted arhats vow to teach in other worlds; Mahaprajapati with nuns gazing, the Buddha's question, her prediction and the nuns'; Yasodhara's thought and prediction; bodhisattvas' verses on abuse, sticks and swords, being called heretics, expulsion by proud monks, not clinging to body or life.
Mahaprajapati described as the Buddha's aunt; Kern's text calls her the Lord's mother's sister. 'Who raised him' deliberately left out of the voice.
Future Buddha names for Mahaprajapati and Yasodhara deliberately left out.
Original: वीर्य (vīrya) is the general term for effort among the perfections; the Sanskrit chapter title may use a different word (utsāha?). Confirm or replace.
